DBinventory

An R package that builds the first two artefacts of a data-documentation effort from a read-only database connection:

  1. Inventory: every table and column, with schema, name, type, row count, size, newest datetime and when it was profiled.
  2. Column profile: per column, the null rate, distinct count, min and max, top values, inferred semantic type (identifier, date, code, free text, flag, …), uniqueness and fingerprint hashes that let copies of the same data be found across tables.

It is general purpose and works over any DBI connection, with dialect support for Microsoft SQL Server (the main target: hospital data warehouses reached over ODBC with SELECT permission only), Parquet files and directories (through DuckDB), DuckDB, SQLite and PostgreSQL. Results go into a SQLite store with per-table checkpointing so a run over hundreds of tables can be interrupted and resumed, and can be exported to CSV or Parquet and rendered as an HTML report from a Quarto template.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ThomUK/DBinventory")

# optional, by source:
install.packages("odbc")    # SQL Server and other ODBC sources
install.packages("duckdb")  # Parquet files and DuckDB databases
install.packages("DT")      # interactive tables in the report

# the synthetic hospital dataset used in the articles and example reports
remotes::install_github("ThomUK/synthetic-hospital-data", subdir = "fakehospdata")

Usage

One call does the whole run:

library(DBinventory)
con <- "Driver={ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server};Server=warehouse;Database=DW;Trusted_Connection=yes;TrustServerCertificate=yes;"

# Sampled report: tables above a million rows are profiled on a sample of their
# rows. Best for a large warehouse, where reading every row of every table
# would take too long for a first look.
out <- inventory_run(con, organisation = "Example NHS Trust",
                     store = "dw_inventory.sqlite", report = "dw_inventory.html")

# Full report: every row of every table. Best when the database is small enough
# to read in full, or when exact distinct counts and uniqueness matter, as they
# do when choosing keys.
out <- inventory_run(con, organisation = "Example NHS Trust", sample_rows = Inf,
                     store = "dw_inventory_full.sqlite", report = "dw_inventory_full.html")

out$inventory$tables   # one row per table or view
out$profile            # one row per column

Other arguments: export_dir writes one CSV per store table (export_format = "parquet" for Parquet), and include, exclude and schema narrow the run to part of the database.

inventory_run() accepts anything db_connect() does: a DBI connection, an ODBC connection string or DSN name, a .sqlite or .duckdb file, a .parquet file or a directory of them.

# a directory of Parquet files, one schema per subdirectory
out <- inventory_run("data/v2/sample", store = "sample_inventory.sqlite")

# the Fake NHS Trust synthetic dataset, for a first look (downloads the 130 MB sample once)
out <- inventory_run(fakehospdata::fh_connect("sample"), store = "fakehosp_inventory.sqlite",
                     organisation = "Fake NHS Trust")

Re-running with the same store resumes: tables already profiled are skipped. Use resume = FALSE to start again.

Step by step 

con <- db_connect("Driver={ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server};Server=...;Database=...;Trusted_Connection=yes;")

tables  <- db_tables(con, schema = "dbo", exclude = "\\.tmp_|_backup$")
inv     <- db_inventory(con, schema = "dbo")           # tables + columns + counts + freshness + sizes
prof    <- db_profile(con, inv, sample_rows = 1e6,     # sample tables above a million rows
                      store = "dw_inventory.sqlite")   # checkpoint per table
dups    <- duplicate_candidates(prof)                  # same data in more than one table?
render_report("dw_inventory.sqlite", "dw_inventory.html")

DBI::dbDisconnect(con)

What the profile holds

Column Meaning
row_count, rows_profiled, sampled, sample_method Full row count from the inventory; how many rows the statistics were computed on and how they were drawn
null_count, null_rate, empty_count Nulls, and empty strings for text columns
distinct_count, distinct_rate, is_unique Distinct values, distinct / non-null, and whether every non-null value is distinct
pk_candidate Unique, never null and a string, integer or uuid type: worth testing as a primary key. On a sampled table this is evidence from the sample only
fk_candidate, fk_target, fk_confidence, fk_evidence, fk_n_targets Best-scoring key column this column appears to reference, from name, range and cardinality evidence (see infer_foreign_keys()); a shortlist for the key register’s match-rate tests, not a confirmed relationship
min_value, max_value, mean_value, true_count Range as text (ISO 8601 for dates), mean for numerics, count of TRUE for booleans
min_length, max_length, mean_length String lengths
top_values, top_values_hash The top_n most frequent values as JSON (read with top_values_of()), and a hash of them
semantic_type identifier, code, category, flag, date, datetime, time, free_text, count, measure, constant, empty, unknown
value_fingerprint, column_fingerprint Hash of what the column holds (type, distinct magnitude, min, max, top values), with and without the normalised column name
values_suppressed Whether literal values were withheld (see below)

Table clusters (phase 2)

On a full run, cluster_tables() groups tables that hold the same data and proposes a canonical member for each group with a one-line rationale, and classes every table as event, reference or aggregate from its own shape. Columns are matched by what they hold (complete value sets for code lists, ranges, distinct rate, value shape, lengths, with name as a secondary signal), and two tables are related only when most of one’s information is in the other and they share a column that is near-unique in both, so a table that merely references another through a foreign key is not mistaken for a copy. The proposals go to a review CSV (decisions = "clusters.csv" in inventory_run()), where the warehouse owners mark each row confirmed or rejected; those decisions override the proposals on later runs. schema_priority = c("layer1", "derived") prefers source-schema tables as canonical where the data alone cannot decide.

Clustering and key inference need exact statistics, so they run only on a full run (sample_rows = Inf). On a sampled run the report’s phase 2 and phase 3 tabs say so.

Key candidates (phase 3)

pk_candidate marks columns that are unique, never null and of a key-like type. fk_candidate and fk_target propose, for each column, the key column in another table it most looks like a reference to, from name evidence, membership in a small key’s complete value set, range containment, cardinality shape and value shape, with fk_confidence from 0 to 1 and fk_evidence spelling out the components. Both are candidates only: the profile cannot see whether a child’s values actually exist in the key, so the shortlist is confirmed or rejected by match-rate tests in the key register stage. The exclusions and the scoring are documented in ?infer_foreign_keys.

Design decisions

These are the choices made where the brief left room; all are easy to change.

Values are suppressed by default. The profile of a hospital warehouse will be committed to a repository, so min_value, max_value and top_values are withheld for columns inferred as free text or as identifiers with more than 200 distinct values, and for columns whose names suggest personal data (nhs, mrn, postcode, dob, name, address, …). Hashes and fingerprints are computed before suppression, so copies still match. Pass keep_values = TRUE where the output itself is held securely.

Large tables are sampled by default. Exact COUNT(*) and MAX(datetime) always run on the full table; value statistics for tables above sample_rows (default a million) are computed on a sample materialised in a session temporary table (TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM on SQL Server, USING SAMPLE ... (system) on DuckDB, ORDER BY random() on SQLite, TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (pct) on PostgreSQL; views on SQL Server fall back to the first rows). sampled and sample_method record what happened. sample_rows = Inf gives the full report.

One query per table for the aggregates, one per eligible column for top values. Aggregates are batched column_batch columns at a time. Top values are skipped for columns with more than top_values_max_distinct distinct values, where a frequency table says little.

Only SELECT is needed. Metadata comes from INFORMATION_SCHEMA (sqlite_master on SQLite). Table sizes come from sys.dm_db_partition_stats on SQL Server and pg_total_relation_size on PostgreSQL when the login can see them, and are NA otherwise. Temporary tables need no extra rights.

Statistics that a type cannot support are skipped, not failed. No MIN() on a SQL Server bit, no COUNT(DISTINCT) on text, ntext, xml or geography; a timestamp on SQL Server is classified as binary (it is a row version). A table that fails for any reason is logged in profile_log and the run continues.

The store is SQLite. It is a single file, needs only RSQLite, and is the checkpoint. store_export() writes CSV (always) or Parquet (with arrow or duckdb).

The report is a Quarto document at inst/report/inventory_report.qmd, rendered with the Quarto CLI when present and otherwise through rmarkdown::render(), which handles the same knitr chunks.

SQL Server notes

  • Connection strings pass straight to odbc::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), .connection_string = ...); a bare name is treated as a DSN. Passwords are redacted before the source is written to run_meta.
  • COUNT_BIG(*) is used for row counts. Datetimes are converted with CONVERT(..., 126) so min, max and freshness are ISO 8601 text.
  • TABLESAMPLE is page based, so a sample is approximately sample_rows rows; the actual number is in rows_profiled.
  • Column names are quoted with square brackets; the odbc driver class (Microsoft SQL Server) selects the dialect. Force it with dialect = "mssql" if a driver reports something else.
  • The package has not yet been run against a live SQL Server from this repository; the T-SQL is covered by unit tests on the generated SQL. The first run against a real warehouse is the next step (see below).

Parquet notes

parquet_connect(dir) exposes a directory as a DuckDB database of views. Each subdirectory is a schema (nested paths joined with _), each file a table. A directory holding two or more Parquet files that share one column schema is read as a single partitioned table (layer1/pas_adt_events/fy2022.parquet, fy2023.parquet become layer1.pas_adt_events). Column types come from the Parquet metadata.

Development

The package is developed against ThomUK/synthetic-hospital-data, read through its fakehospdata package. The tests run offline on tests/testthat/fixtures/fakehosp_tiny.sqlite, 45 tables and a view capped at 200 rows with declared types preserved, built from the sample by the script beside it. The articles and the example reports on the site use the real sample and full sets; the example reports are regenerated by the example-reports workflow on the Actions tab.

python3 tests/testthat/fixtures/build_fixture.py path/to/synthetic-hospital-data/data/v2/sample tests/testthat/fixtures/fakehosp_tiny.sqlite 200
Rscript -e 'devtools::test()'
Rscript -e 'rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck()'

Roadmap

The sequence from an inherited, undocumented database to one that is under control and useful, which phases this package covers and what comes next, is set out in the roadmap article. In short: inventory and profile (built), collapse to the canonical set (next), keys and structure, documentation of the canonical set, control, then the semantic model.
